key_insight: Multi-agent collaboration is not always better: for stronger language models, adding more agents can eventually reduce performance rather than improve it. The paper shows when collaboration helps, when it hurts, and that a predictive selector can choose the best architecture with strong accuracy.
problem_solved: AI practitioners often assume that more agents or more collaboration will automatically improve LLM performance, but the best setup depends on the task and model capability. This paper addresses how to predict the right multi-agent architecture instead of relying on trial and error.
method: Evaluated large language model agents across 260 controlled configurations to compare single-agent and multi-agent setups.
Measured when collaboration improved outcomes versus when it introduced overhead, conflict, or degraded performance.
Trained a predictive model to recommend the best architecture and tested it on held-out within-domain configurations.
impact: This helps researchers and engineers design agent systems more effectively, saving time and compute by avoiding unhelpful collaboration patterns. It also provides a practical decision tool for selecting whether to use one agent or many for a given task.
visual_elements: A decision tree showing when to use single-agent vs multi-agent setups
A line chart illustrating performance gains and collapse as model capability increases
A grid/heatmap of the 260 configurations with color-coded outcomes
An accuracy gauge or confusion matrix for the predictive architecture selector
paper_title: Capable language models can outgrow the benefits of collaboration
paper_authors: Yubin Kim, Ken Gu, Chanwoo Park, Chunjong Park, Samuel Schmidgall
